subject: ela
description: Students use knowledge of language and its conventions when writing, speaking, reading, and listening. They vary sentence patterns for meaning, reader or listener interest, and style, and they maintain consistency in style and tone across a piece of writing. They judge how a particular word choice, sentence structure, level of formality, or revision affects clarity, emphasis, and the impression on an audience, and they choose the option that best fits the writer's purpose and situation. Every item embeds the full sentence or short passage it depends on, so the student needs nothing external.
subSkills: Vary sentence patterns (combining short sentences, splitting run-ons, changing sentence openers) to improve flow, reader interest, and emphasis
Recognize and maintain a consistent style and tone within a piece of writing, and spot a sentence that breaks that consistency
Match level of formality and word choice to audience, purpose, and situation (formal essay vs. friendly note vs. spoken request)
Evaluate how a specific word choice or revision changes the meaning, emphasis, or impression a sentence or passage makes
Choose the most effective revision among several grammatically correct options based on clarity, conciseness, and purpose

problemArchetypes.name: Combine sentences for better flow
problemArchetypes.example: Read the pair: 'The storm knocked out the power. The whole neighborhood went dark.' Which revision combines these most effectively without losing meaning? Answer: 'When the storm knocked out the power, the whole neighborhood went dark,' because it shows the cause-and-effect link in one smooth sentence.

problemArchetypes.name: Vary sentence openers for interest
problemArchetypes.example: Read the passage: 'I woke up late. I missed the bus. I ran to school. I arrived sweaty.' Why does this passage feel choppy, and which revision improves it? Answer: every sentence starts the same way and is the same length; varying the openers and combining ideas, such as 'Because I woke up late, I missed the bus and had to run to school, arriving sweaty,' creates better flow.

problemArchetypes.name: Maintain consistent tone or style
problemArchetypes.example: Read the passage from a formal report: 'The experiment produced clear results. The data showed a steady increase. Honestly, it was super cool to watch.' Which sentence breaks the formal tone, and how should it be revised? Answer: 'Honestly, it was super cool to watch' is too casual; revise to 'The increase was striking to observe.'

problemArchetypes.name: Match formality to audience and purpose
problemArchetypes.example: Read the situation: A student is emailing a teacher to ask for a deadline extension. Which sentence is most appropriate? Answer: 'Would it be possible to have an extra day to complete the assignment?' rather than 'Hey, can I get more time?' because the formal, polite phrasing fits writing to a teacher.

problemArchetypes.name: Evaluate the effect of a word choice or revision
problemArchetypes.example: Read the sentence: 'The dog moved across the yard.' How does changing 'moved' to 'bolted' affect the sentence? Answer: 'bolted' adds speed and urgency, giving the reader a sharper, more energetic picture than the neutral word 'moved.'

Easy.description: A single short sentence or a two-sentence pair (roughly 8 to 20 words total) embedded in the item. The task is identify-level: pick the smoother combination of two short sentences, choose the more vivid or appropriate word, or spot the one sentence that sounds too casual. The better choice is clear and only one language concept is tested.
constraints: Stimulus is one short sentence or a two-sentence pair included in the prompt
Tests exactly one concept (sentence combining OR word choice OR obvious formality mismatch)
Identify-level task: select the more effective option from a clear set
No multi-step reasoning; the best answer is plainly stronger than the others

Medium.description: A compound or complex sentence, or a short two to three sentence passage (roughly 20 to 40 words), embedded in the item. The task is analyze-level: choose the revision that best varies sentence structure for flow, identify and fix the sentence that breaks tone consistency, or match phrasing to a stated audience and purpose. Distractors are grammatically correct but less effective, so the student must compare options rather than reject an obvious error.
constraints: Stimulus is a compound/complex sentence or a two to three sentence passage in the prompt
Tests sentence variety, tone consistency, or audience-and-purpose matching
Analyze-level task: compare several correct options and choose the most effective
Distractors are plausible and grammatically correct but weaker in flow, tone, or fit

Hard.description: A short multi-sentence passage (roughly 4 to 6 sentences, 50 to 80 words) embedded in the item that contains interacting issues of style, tone, sentence variety, or formality. The task is evaluate-level: judge which full revision best serves a stated purpose and audience, explain why one word choice or structure creates a stronger impression than another, or fix a passage where a tone break and a choppy structure occur together. Requires inference about the writer's intent and the audience's likely reaction.
constraints: Stimulus is a 4 to 6 sentence passage included in the prompt
Contains interacting issues (tone plus sentence variety, or formality plus emphasis)
Evaluate-level task: select the best full revision and justify the language choice
Requires inference about the writer's purpose and the effect on a specific audience

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student equates 'more words' or 'longer sentences' with better writing and chooses a wordy, padded revision over a clear concise one
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects 'Due to the fact that it was raining at that point in time, we made the decision to stay inside' instead of the tighter 'Because it was raining, we stayed inside'

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student thinks varying sentences means making every sentence long and complex, turning clear ideas into one tangled run-on
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects a single overloaded sentence that crams four ideas together instead of a balanced mix of sentence lengths

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student ignores tone consistency and accepts a casual or slang sentence inside a formal passage because each sentence is grammatically correct on its own
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Keeps 'Honestly, it was super cool to watch' in a formal report instead of revising it to match the formal tone

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student mismatches formality to the audience, choosing overly casual phrasing for a formal situation or stiff, unnatural phrasing for a friendly one
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects 'Hey, can I get more time?' for an email to a teacher, or 'I am writing to formally request your presence' for a text to a friend

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student judges word choice only by whether the word is 'fancy' rather than whether it fits the intended meaning and impression
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Replaces a neutral verb with a dramatic one that distorts the meaning, choosing 'demolished' for a gentle action because it sounds more impressive

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student picks the first grammatically correct option and stops, without comparing how each option affects clarity, emphasis, or flow
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects an accurate but choppy or flat version over a smoother, more purposeful revision because both are technically correct
